title: Formula money and pass-through 101: when the door is the state
one_liner: Much federal programme money goes by formula to a state, tribe or local body, which then funds local organisations through subawards [1280](#cite:1280) [1292](#cite:1292).
why_here: The section on funding a programme or a service and the formula route assume the reader knows why a federal page names a state office. A newcomer looks for a federal application that the programme does not have.

## What it is

A non-profit that finds a federal programme paying for its kind of work tends to assume that the next step is an application to the agency named on the page. On the formula route no such step exists [1292](#cite:1292) [1259](#cite:1259). Federal awards divide by how the recipient and the amount are chosen [1880](#cite:1880). For a [discretionary grant](#term:discretionary-grant) the agency may select the recipient from among all eligible applicants and decides the amount [1880](#cite:1880). A [formula grant](#term:formula-grant) is an allocation to states, territories or local governments by a distribution formula in the law or regulations [1880](#cite:1880). Agencies call some of these [block grants](#term:block-grant), a term for which the [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) glossary had no entry when read on October 4, 2026 [1292](#cite:1292) [1880](#cite:1880).

The body that receives the money then funds local organisations, and the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) names each party [1292](#cite:1292) [1799](#cite:1799). A [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) is a recipient or [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) that gives a [subaward](#term:subaward) to another organisation to carry out part of a federal programme [1799](#cite:1799). The organisation that receives the subaward is a subrecipient, and the award terms flow down to it [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). A non-profit funded through a state block or formula grant is a subrecipient of the state [1823](#cite:1823) [1880](#cite:1880).

HUD's page for the Community Development Block Grant says so in plain words: "HUD does not provide CDBG assistance directly to individuals, businesses, nonprofit or organizations or other non-governmental entities." [1292](#cite:1292) FEMA's FY 2026 notice for the Nonprofit Security [Grant](#term:grant) Program reads: "Nonprofit organizations may NOT apply directly to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)/FEMA." [1320](#cite:1320) The Administration for Community Living writes that formula grants "require no application or competition" [1259](#cite:1259). The two [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa) block grants, [HRSA](#term:hrsa)'s [Title V](#term:title-iii-v-eligibility) block grant and the Education Department's 21st Century Community Learning Centers are awarded to states in the same way [1130](#cite:1130) [1168](#cite:1168) [1399](#cite:1399). Past that point the federal pages read for the health block grants do not describe how a provider applies to its state [1129](#cite:1129) [1168](#cite:1168) [1219](#cite:1219).

Under 2 CFR 200.332 a pass-through entity verifies in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) that the subrecipient is not excluded, identifies the subaward as a subaward with 14 data items, evaluates the subrecipient's risk of fraud and of noncompliance, monitors its activities, reviews its reports and verifies that it is audited when the rules require [1823](#cite:1823) [2105](#cite:2105). A state that distributes a formula grant has the same list of duties as a university that leads a multi-site project [1823](#cite:1823). The guidance does not reach every such grant in full: 2 CFR 200.101(e) takes block grants authorised by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 out of subparts C, D and E of the guidance, except for specified provisions [1805](#cite:1805).

title: Foundations 101: kinds of foundation and how each takes a request
one_liner: A foundation is a class in tax law, not a small federal agency, and each one states for itself how it takes a request [2237](#cite:2237) [2124](#cite:2124).
why_here: Section 7, the foundation routes and every foundation funder record assume this idea. A newcomer trips by expecting an open application form at each foundation and a federal indirect cost rate in each budget.
body_before:
## What it is

A newcomer who has read a federal funding notice tends to treat a foundation as a small agency, with a published programme and a form open to anyone eligible. The law starts somewhere else. Under the tax code every [section 501(c)(3)](#term:section-501c3) organisation is a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) unless it falls into a category the law excludes [2237](#cite:2237). The excluded organisations are the [public charities](#term:public-charity): churches, hospitals, schools, colleges and universities, organisations with many sources of support, and organisations that support them [2238](#cite:2238). A private foundation files [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) each year and is subject to excise taxes that a public charity is not [2237](#cite:2237) [2387](#cite:2387). That return is public and lists every [grant](#term:grant) paid [2387](#cite:2387) [2461](#cite:2461).

The names a grant seeker meets sort into a few kinds. The foundations this guide's records label independent or family, Sloan and Moore for example, are private foundations that file Form 990-PF [2126](#cite:2126) [2132](#cite:2132). IRS statistics call the grantmaking kind nonoperating; it filed 91.2% of private foundation returns for tax year 2022 [2410](#cite:2410). That kind must pay out a minimum each year, computed from 5 percent of its investment assets [2375](#cite:2375) [2377](#cite:2377). An [operating foundation](#term:operating-foundation) devotes most of its resources to its own activities and is not subject to the tax on failure to distribute income [2371](#cite:2371). A [corporate foundation](#term:corporate-foundation) is a private foundation whose assets come mainly from a for-profit business; a company may also give through a programme inside the company, which files no public return of its own [2408](#cite:2408) [2387](#cite:2387). A [community foundation](#term:community-foundation) that meets a public support test is a public charity and files [Form 990](#term:form-990) [2374](#cite:2374). So do some national grantmakers: The Pew Charitable Trusts files Form 990, and HHMI's audited statements for fiscal year 2023 call it a public charity [2176](#cite:2176) [2486](#cite:2486). Congress created others to sit beside a federal agency, among them the Foundation for the [National Institutes of Health](#term:nih) in 1990 and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation in 1984 [2448](#cite:2448) [2452](#cite:2452).

Each foundation states on its own pages how it takes requests, and this guide records the answers of 65 foundations and other private grantmakers [2124](#cite:2124) [2290](#cite:2290). The 65 are an editorial sample chosen by the editor, not a ranking, and the counts that follow were made from those records. Six accept [unsolicited requests](#term:unsolicited-request), among them The Duke Endowment, the Cleveland Foundation and The New York Community Trust [2310](#cite:2310) [2426](#cite:2426) [2418](#cite:2418). Ten begin with a [letter of inquiry](#term:letter-of-inquiry), a short first document after which, in Carnegie Corporation's words, "applicants may be invited via email to submit a full proposal"; Sloan and the Commonwealth Fund work the same way [2216](#cite:2216) [2124](#cite:2124) [2323](#cite:2323). Twenty-three take applications only under an [open call](#term:open-call) they have posted, as Simons, Spencer and Knight do [2119](#cite:2119) [2196](#cite:2196) [2296](#cite:2296). Twenty-three fund [by invitation only](#term:invitation-only). Ford's page reads "We do not accept any unsolicited grant proposals by mail, email or phone." [2259](#cite:2259) Mott has not accepted unsolicited letters of inquiry or proposals since January 2025 [2298](#cite:2298). For three no answer is recorded: the Chicago Community Trust, the Foundation for the NIH and the National Park Foundation [2423](#cite:2423) [2448](#cite:2448) [2455](#cite:2455).

Many foundation fellowships cannot be applied for directly: the institution nominates under a cap the funder sets, and so chooses among its own faculty before the funder sees anything [2174](#cite:2174) [2175](#cite:2175). Dreyfus takes one [nomination](#term:institutional-nomination) per institution a year for each programme, and Packard took up to two from each of 50 invited institutions in 2026 [2146](#cite:2146) [2147](#cite:2147) [2149](#cite:2149). Money for organisations comes in two main kinds. [General operating support](#term:general-operating-support) pays for an organisation's work as a whole; [project support](#term:project-grant) pays for one named piece of work with its own budget [2261](#cite:2261). Hewlett gives general operating support whenever possible; Woodruff says most of its grants support one-time needs [2280](#cite:2280) [2313](#cite:2313).

The first picture is a row of five doors, labelled from left to right in the foundations' terms, each with its count: unsolicited requests accepted, six; letter of inquiry first, ten; open calls only, twenty-three; invitation only, twenty-three; not stated, three [2310](#cite:2310) [2216](#cite:2216) [2119](#cite:2119) [2211](#cite:2211) [2448](#cite:2448). Beneath the doors a small check box is drawn, because the tax return asks the same question. Part XIV, line 2 of the 2025 Form 990-PF has a box for a foundation that "only makes contributions to preselected charitable organizations and does not accept unsolicited requests for funds"; one that leaves it unchecked gives a contact, a form of application, deadlines and restrictions on lines 2a to 2d [2387](#cite:2387). The box is the foundation's own statement for the tax year of the return, and its website may say something newer [2387](#cite:2387). A community foundation files Form 990 and has no such line [2374](#cite:2374). Returns can be read free on the IRS [Tax Exempt Organization Search](#term:tax-exempt-organization-search) and on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer [2059](#cite:2059) [2398](#cite:2398).

The second picture is a scale of percentages starting at zero, with each foundation's [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) figure marked on it. A foundation does not pay a university's federally [negotiated rate](#term:nicra); each sets its own limit, and there is no common rule [2120](#cite:2120) [2133](#cite:2133) [2129](#cite:2129) [2156](#cite:2156). Two marks are drawn differently because they are not ceilings: Ford's 25 percent is a minimum on project grants, and MacArthur adds a flat 29 percent to project costs; neither rate applies to general operating support [2332](#cite:2332) [2265](#cite:2265). A note marks a different base: Pew's limit is 8 percent of the total award [2174](#cite:2174).

title: Grants, cooperative agreements and contracts 101
one_liner: A federal award is a legal instrument that statute selects, and a separate division decides whether anyone competes for it before an agency.
why_here: The first two sections of the main text, every route and every programme record assume the reader can tell a competed grant from formula money and from a project Congress names. Newcomers trip because one word, grant, is used for all of them.

further_reading.title: 31 U.S.C. chapter 63, Using Procurement Contracts and Grant and Cooperative Agreements (sections 6301-6308)
House Appropriations Committee Guidance for Community Project Funding (FY 2027)

body_before:
## What it is

A newcomer tends to call any money from a federal agency a [grant](#term:grant), and to assume that getting one means beating other applicants. Federal law treats an award as a legal instrument and gives an agency three of them, the choice following from the purpose of the transaction [1851](#cite:1851). A [procurement contract](#term:procurement-contract) acquires property or services for the Government's own direct benefit or use [1851](#cite:1851). A grant and a [cooperative agreement](#term:cooperative-agreement) both transfer something of value to carry out a public purpose that a law authorises [1851](#cite:1851).

Those two differ on one point: whether substantial involvement is expected between the agency and the recipient while the work is carried out [1851](#cite:1851). The statute does not define that involvement, so a notice for a cooperative agreement has to describe what the agency expects [1848](#cite:1848). At [NIH](#term:nih) the [U01](#term:u01) funds a research project under a cooperative agreement [49](#cite:49) [3](#cite:3). One U01 notice says that after award NIH staff "will assist, guide, coordinate, or participate in project activities", and it sends disputes to a three-member panel [116](#cite:116).

A second division cuts across the first. The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) defines a [discretionary award](#term:discretionary-grant) as one in which the agency, under statutory authority to exercise judgment, selects the recipient or the amount through a competitive process or on the merit of proposals [1894](#cite:1894). A non-discretionary award goes to specific recipients under statutory requirements, such that the agency cannot exercise judgment [1894](#cite:1894). [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov)'s glossary describes a [mandatory grant](#term:formula-grant), where the authorising statute requires an award to each eligible entity, and a formula grant, an allocation to states, territories or local governments by a formula in the law [1880](#cite:1880). A discretionary award is competed before a federal agency; formula money is reached, if at all, through a state or local recipient [1880](#cite:1880) [1805](#cite:1805). Each programme's entry in the [Assistance Listings](#term:assistance-listing), the government-wide source of information on [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) programmes, states which kind its awards are [1808](#cite:1808). A project named by Congress is a further case. Congress may name a recipient, a project and an amount in an [appropriations act](#term:appropriations-act), which the House calls [Community Project Funding](#term:community-project-funding) and the Senate Congressionally Directed Spending [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674). No organisation applies to either committee, and a named recipient still applies to the agency before money moves [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674) [1686](#cite:1686).

Whatever the instrument, what arrives is a document. At NIH the [Notice of Award](#term:notice-of-award) is the official award document, and the recipient accepts it by drawing down or requesting funds [122](#cite:122). The [period of performance](#term:budget-period) is the time between the start and end date of an award and may contain one or more budget periods; a budget period is the funded portion during which the recipient is authorised to incur financial obligations [1799](#cite:1799). Both pairs of dates are printed in the award document [1810](#cite:1810). An [R01](#term:r01) is generally awarded for one to five budget periods, each normally 12 months [42](#cite:42). Funding for each later budget period is a [continuation](#term:continuation): one [HHS](#term:hhs) notice has recipients file a non-competing continuation application for each later budget period, and NIH's annual [progress report](#term:rppr) is due about 45 or about 60 days before the next one starts, depending on the award [1218](#cite:1218) [1954](#cite:1954). A [renewal](#term:renewal) is different. An R01 "can be renewed by competing for an additional project period", and a renewal award begins a new and distinct period of performance [42](#cite:42) [1816](#cite:1816).
picture:
Picture two questions, one drawn above the other. The upper one asks what the transaction is for, and it has two branches. Where the Government acquires property or services for its own direct benefit or use, the branch ends in a box labelled procurement contract [1851](#cite:1851). Where something of value is transferred for a public purpose, the branch forks once more on whether substantial involvement is expected, into a box labelled grant where it is not and a box labelled cooperative agreement where it is [1851](#cite:1851).

The lower question asks who chooses the recipient, and three boxes stand side by side beneath it. In the box labelled discretionary the agency selects from among eligible applicants [1880](#cite:1880). In the box labelled mandatory or formula the authorising statute sets who is paid and how much, and an arrow runs on to a state, territory or local government [1880](#cite:1880). In the third box Congress names the recipient: an arrow enters from the office of a House Member or a Senator, and another leaves towards the agency, where the named recipient still applies [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674) [1686](#cite:1686). An award has a place on each line at once [1851](#cite:1851) [1880](#cite:1880).

## How this guide uses it

Each programme record names the instrument it funds by, and formula programmes carry their own [status label](#term:status-label). The section on how grant money moves starts from the two divisions drawn here, and the section on programme and service money follows the formula box to the state. The routes divide along the lower line as well, with one route kept for a project named by Congress. The figure of the four doors adds foundations to the three boxes of that line. The primer on reading a funding notice takes up the discretionary box from this point.


Two things were unsettled on October 5, 2026. [OMB](#term:omb)'s [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of May 29, 2026 would revise 2 CFR 200.201, the section on the choice of instrument, and would remove one form of grant, the fixed amount award [1803](#cite:1803). It is a proposal: the [continuing resolution](#term:continuing-resolution) approved September 2, 2026 bars a rule arising from it from being issued or finalised through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). Under the same resolution NIH states that its institutes may issue non-competing awards "at a level below that indicated on the most recent Notice of Award" [83](#cite:83).

title: Indirect costs 101: the rate, the base, and the two fifteen percents
one_liner: Indirect costs are paid as a rate applied to a base of direct costs; the de minimis rate is up to 15 percent [1802](#cite:1802) [1849](#cite:1849).
why_here: Budget terms in the programme records, the two indirect-cost figures and the ledger of changes all assume a reader knows what a rate and a base are. The newcomer's trap is the figure of 15 percent, which names two unrelated rules.

body_before:
## What it is

A newcomer drawing up a first budget tends to treat the award as the cost of the project: the salaries and the supplies. Those are [direct costs](#term:direct-costs), the ones that can be identified specifically with the award [1835](#cite:1835). On top of them come [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs): costs incurred for a common or joint purpose that cannot readily be assigned to the award that benefits [1799](#cite:1799). At major universities and major non-profits they fall into two groups, Facilities and Administration, which gives the other name, F&A costs [1802](#cite:1802).

The second amount is worked out as a percentage, the indirect cost rate, applied to a base of direct costs [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850). An organisation gets its rate in one of two ways [1802](#cite:1802). One is a [negotiated indirect cost rate agreement](#term:nicra), settled by a single federal agency, the organisation's [cognizant agency for indirect costs](#term:cognizant-agency), on behalf of all the others, which must then accept it [1799](#cite:1799) [1802](#cite:1802). For a university that agency is [HHS](#term:hhs) or the Office of Naval Research; for a non-profit it is the agency with the largest dollar value of awards made directly to the organisation [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850). The other way is the [de minimis rate](#term:de-minimis-rate): an organisation with no current negotiated rate may elect up to 15 percent of [modified total direct costs](#term:mtdc), without documentation, and use it indefinitely [1802](#cite:1802). Agency pages do not all carry that figure, and the [NIH](#term:nih) policy text as fetched gives 10% [64](#cite:64).

The base is normally modified total direct costs, or MTDC [1799](#cite:1799). It takes in salaries and wages, fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each [subaward](#term:subaward) [1799](#cite:1799). Equipment, capital expenditures, patient care charges, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, [participant support costs](#term:participant-support-costs) and the rest of each subaward are left out [1799](#cite:1799).

A negotiated rate does not reach every award. An agency may use a different rate when a federal statute or regulation requires it, and HHS regulations limit indirect costs on [training grants](#term:t32) to 8% of MTDC [1802](#cite:1802) [1884](#cite:1884). NIH pays that 8% on [K awards](#term:k-award) and T32 training grants [744](#cite:744) [750](#cite:750). Its individual fellowships and [S10](#term:s10) instrument awards pay none [736](#cite:736) [1536](#cite:1536). Foundations follow no common rule, and each sets its own figure in its own policy [2129](#cite:2129) [2156](#cite:2156). Gates allows U.S. universities up to 10% of budgeted total direct costs, and Ford sets a minimum of 25 percent on its project [grants](#term:grant) [2257](#cite:2257) [2332](#cite:2332).

The unshaded segment is labelled *left out of the base* and lists equipment, tuition remission and participant support costs, among others [1799](#cite:1799). A bracket over the shaded segment alone reads *rate × base*, and a further segment joined to the end of the bar, labelled *indirect costs*, is as long as that product [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850).

Two tags, each marked *15 percent*, hang beneath. The first points at the bracket and reads *de minimis rate: an option for an organisation with no negotiated rate; in force* [1802](#cite:1802). The second points at a separate box, *2025 caps on negotiated rates: NIH, DOE, [NSF](#term:nsf), DoD; none in effect on October 4, 2026* [24](#cite:24) [237](#cite:237) [289](#cite:289) [1855](#cite:1855). A shorter bar drawn below, labelled *foundation grant*, carries its own bracket marked *the foundation's own figure* [2129](#cite:2129).

## The maths, gently

$$ \text{indirect costs} = \text{rate} \times \text{base}, \qquad \text{base} = \text{MTDC} $$

- **Indirect costs**: the amount the award pays on top of direct costs [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850).
- **Rate**: the organisation's negotiated rate, or the de minimis rate of up to 15 percent [1802](#cite:1802).
- **Base**: modified total direct costs, the direct costs that remain once the excluded items are taken out [1799](#cite:1799).

A worked example, with illustrative direct costs. An organisation with no negotiated rate budgets $100,000 for salaries, fringe benefits, supplies and travel, $20,000 for one piece of equipment and $80,000 for one subaward; all three figures are illustrative. The equipment is left out of the base, and only the first $50,000 of the subaward counts [1799](#cite:1799). The base is therefore $150,000. At a de minimis rate of 15 percent, the most the rule allows, the indirect costs are $22,500 [1802](#cite:1802). Direct costs remain $200,000 in all, and the award comes to $222,500.

## How this guide uses it

Section 3 of the main text sets out these rules. The programme records state the indirect cost terms of each programme, the routes for training awards and foundation grants depend on the limits described here, and two figures, indirect-cost-rules and foundation-indirect-rates, set the federal rules, the 2025 caps and the foundations' figures side by side.


The second 15 percent is contested. In 2025 four agencies announced that they would pay universities indirect costs at 15 percent in place of negotiated rates, and the District of Massachusetts set each policy aside [24](#cite:24) [1852](#cite:1852) [237](#cite:237) [1855](#cite:1855). NIH's notice of February 7, 2025 was [enjoined](#term:injunction) and later [vacated](#term:vacatur), and the First Circuit affirmed on January 5, 2026 [24](#cite:24). DOE's policy of April 11, 2025 was vacated on June 30, 2025, and DOE declared it no longer in effect from January 23, 2026 [1852](#cite:1852) [289](#cite:289). NSF's notice of May 2, 2025 was vacated on June 20, 2025; a case summary records that the First Circuit dismissed NSF's appeal, on NSF's own motion, on September 30, 2025 [1854](#cite:1854) [239](#cite:239). The Department of Defense memoranda of May 14 and June 12, 2025 were vacated on October 10, 2025, with a permanent injunction for the university plaintiffs and the member universities of the plaintiff associations; a plaintiff association reports that the Government's appeal was dismissed on February 18, 2026 [1855](#cite:1855) [292](#cite:292). [Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332) directs [OMB](#term:omb) to revise the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) to limit facilities and administrative costs, and no such revision has taken effect [246](#cite:246) [1480](#cite:1480).

title: Law in motion 101: reading a rule that is being fought over

## What it is

A newcomer would take an agency's announcement for the rule. In 2025 and 2026 an announcement was often one layer of law among several, and another layer undid it. Congress enacts statutes, numbered as public laws; Public Law 119-103 was approved on September 2, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). A regulation sits in the [Code of Federal Regulations](#term:cfr), where the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) is 2 CFR part 200, and a federal statute governs where it conflicts with that part [1805](#cite:1805). A regulation changes through the [Federal Register](#term:federal-register): the text of part 200 in force was published there on April 22, 2024 at 89 FR 30046 and took effect on October 1, 2024 [1883](#cite:1883).

A [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) is a draft published for comment. [OMB](#term:omb) published one on May 29, 2026, at 91 FR 32198, to revise 2 CFR; comments were due July 13, 2026, and the Federal Register record shows 496,606 of them [1458](#cite:1458) [1858](#cite:1858). Until a [final rule](#term:final-rule) is published, the proposal applies to no one [1480](#cite:1480) [1803](#cite:1803). An [executive order](#term:executive-order) is the President's instruction to agencies: [Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332), signed August 7, 2025, directs OMB to revise the Uniform Guidance, and no such revision has taken effect [246](#cite:246) [1480](#cite:1480). An agency notice states that agency's policy. [NIH](#term:nih)'s notice of February 7, 2025 announced a standard 15% [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) rate in place of [negotiated rates](#term:nicra), and DOE, [NSF](#term:nsf) and the Department of Defense announced the same rate for [institutions of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) on April 11, May 2 and May 14, 2025 [25](#cite:25) [1852](#cite:1852) [237](#cite:237) [1855](#cite:1855).

An [injunction](#term:injunction) is a court order that bars an agency from acting, for the parties the order covers; a [vacatur](#term:vacatur) sets the policy itself aside. The District of Massachusetts enjoined NIH's notice on March 5, 2025, later made the injunction permanent and vacated the notice, and [on appeal](#term:on-appeal) the First Circuit affirmed on January 5, 2026 [24](#cite:24). The same court vacated NSF's policy on June 20, 2025 without an injunction [1854](#cite:1854). It enjoined DOE's on May 15, 2025, in an order not limited to the named plaintiffs, and vacated it on June 30, 2025 [1853](#cite:1853) [1852](#cite:1852). It vacated the Defense policy on October 10, 2025 and made its injunction permanent for the university plaintiffs and the member universities of the plaintiff associations [1855](#cite:1855). The [HHS](#term:hhs) notices of March 24 and 25, 2025 [terminated](#term:termination) about $11 billion in [CDC](#term:cdc) and [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa) public health [grants](#term:grant) [544](#cite:544). The injunction of May 16, 2025, granted to twenty-three states and the District of Columbia, bars HHS "from enforcing or implementing the public health terminations for Plaintiff States and their local health jurisdictions" [544](#cite:544).

An [appropriations act](#term:appropriations-act) is the statute that funds agencies for a fiscal year, and it can carry conditions: section 224 of the FY 2026 act, Public Law 119-75, keeps the indirect cost provisions of 45 CFR part 75 applying to NIH grants [62](#cite:62). A [continuing resolution](#term:continuing-resolution) extends the prior year's acts for a limited time, as Public Law 119-103 does through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). A [budget request](#term:budget-request) is a proposal to Congress. The FY 2027 President's Budget proposes a [15 percent cap](#term:indirect-rate-cap) on F&A costs for each NIH award [57](#cite:57). In May 2025 the White House proposed eliminating the [Legal Services Corporation](#term:legal-services-corporation) in FY 2026, and Congress passed $540 million for it [1329](#cite:1329).

Picture a time line from January 2025 to December 2026, with a row for each contested rule and a mark for each event, shaped by who acted: an agency, a court, Congress or the President. The row for NIH's indirect cost cap reads: notice, February 7, 2025; injunction, March 5, 2025; affirmed on appeal, January 5, 2026; appropriations act with section 224, signed February 3, 2026 [25](#cite:25) [24](#cite:24) [62](#cite:62). The row for the Uniform Guidance reads: proposed rule, May 29, 2026; comments closed, July 13, 2026; section 157 of Public Law 119-103, September 2, 2026. A shaded band then runs to December 11, 2026, the date through which no rule arising from the proposal may be issued or finalised [1458](#cite:1458) [1480](#cite:1480).

Beside each mark stands a status word from the guide's change records, and each word is learned most easily from a record that carries it. *Announced* marks a statement of plans, such as the three tranches of FY 2027 competitions [IES](#term:ies) set out on August 6, 2026 [661](#cite:661). *Proposed* marks OMB's rule and the FY 2027 budget requests [1458](#cite:1458) [57](#cite:57). *Enacted* marks an appropriation Congress has passed, *final* an action issued and standing, such as the NIH award terms effective October 1, 2025, and *[pending-implementation](#term:pending-implementation)* an action issued with a later start, such as NIH's letters of collaboration, due in fiscal year 2027 [1329](#cite:1329) [65](#cite:65) [131](#cite:131). *Enjoined* marks the HHS terminations and *vacated* the NIH cap [544](#cite:544) [24](#cite:24). *In-litigation* marks a dispute still before a court, such as the suit Tennessee and Students for Fair Admissions filed on June 11, 2025 over three Education Department programmes [1607](#cite:1607). *On-appeal* marks a ruling under review: the Ninth Circuit ruled in Thakur v. Trump on May 26, 2026, and the government petitioned the Supreme Court in August 2026 [242](#cite:242) [243](#cite:243). *[Rescinded](#term:rescission)* marks a step its issuer withdrew, as NIH did on June 12, 2025 with a civil rights award term added on April 21, 2025 [1870](#cite:1870) [1871](#cite:1871). *Frozen-by-appropriations* marks section 157 [1480](#cite:1480).

## What it is

A newcomer might take a funding notice for an advertisement that each agency lays out as it likes. A [notice of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) is the formal announcement that federal funding is available through a [financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) programme, and the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) fixes what it must contain and in what order [1799](#cite:1799) [1800](#cite:1800) [1848](#cite:1848). Those rules cover discretionary programmes [1800](#cite:1800). The full text has nine sections: Basic Information; Eligibility; Program Description; Application Contents and Format; Submission Requirements and Deadlines; Application Review Information; Award Notices; Post-Award Requirements and Administration; and Other Information, which is optional [1848](#cite:1848).

Ahead of the full text comes a summary, displayed on [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) [1800](#cite:1800). It gives the agency name, the opportunity title, the announcement type, the [funding opportunity number](#term:opportunity-number), the [Assistance Listing number](#term:assistance-listing), funding details, key dates, an executive summary and agency contacts [1800](#cite:1800). The opportunity number identifies the notice: PA-25-301 is [NIH](#term:nih)'s parent [R01](#term:r01) notice [4](#cite:4). The Assistance Listing number points to something else, the programme's entry in the public catalogue of federal assistance programmes kept by the General Services Administration at [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov), and the same number is printed in the award document [1799](#cite:1799) [1808](#cite:1808) [1810](#cite:1810).

Inside the full text, the Eligibility section has to list every type of eligible applicant [1848](#cite:1848). The dates show how long a notice stays open. The guidance sets a standard of at least 60 calendar days and a floor of 30 absent exigent circumstances, though the paragraph states an expectation, not a requirement [1800](#cite:1800). [Cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing), also called matching, is the part of project cost not paid by federal funds; the notice must state whether it is required, and say so when it is not [1880](#cite:1880) [1848](#cite:1848). The [application package](#term:application-package) is the set of forms the opportunity requires, loaded into its Workspace on Grants.gov, where a team fills them in before an [Authorized Organization Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative) submits [1918](#cite:1918) [1915](#cite:1915). Among the forms is the [SF-424](#term:sf-424), the standard federal application form, issued in several sets [1918](#cite:1918).

NIH and [NSF](#term:nsf) each depart from the picture of one notice with one deadline. NIH's ordinary route is the [parent announcement](#term:parent-announcement), a standing, broad notice for an application whose topic the investigator chose, and each is for one [activity code](#term:activity-code) [1](#cite:1) [145](#cite:145). An activity code has three characters, the first usually marking the funding category: R for research, T for training, F for fellowship, K for career development [3](#cite:3). The notice stays open for years while applications arrive on standard due dates, three a year for each code [2](#cite:2). PA-25-301 was posted December 18, 2024; its NIH page gives an expiration date of January 08, 2028 and its Grants.gov listing a close date of January 7, 2028 [4](#cite:4) [112](#cite:112). NSF publishes four kinds of opportunity [156](#cite:156). A programme description and a programme announcement use the generic rules of its policy guide; a [programme solicitation](#term:program-solicitation) is more focused, applies for a limited period and is used when NSF departs from those rules, for instance by limiting who may submit [156](#cite:156) [158](#cite:158). A [Dear Colleague Letter](#term:dear-colleague-letter) gives information or announces interest in a topic [156](#cite:156) [158](#cite:158). Each NSF opportunity sets its own timing: a deadline date, a target date, a submission window or acceptance at any time [156](#cite:156).
picture:
Picture one line running left to right, the life of a single listing on Grants.gov, with four marks on it. The marks carry the four values of the site's status filter: [forecasted](#term:forecast), posted, closed, archived [2536](#cite:2536). At Forecasted the listing gives estimated dates: the forecast for a [NIOSH](#term:cdc) [R21](#term:r21-r03) notice, RFA-OH-27-033, gave a forecast posted date of July 27, 2026, an estimated post date of December 16, 2026 and an estimated application due date of February 16, 2027 [2535](#cite:2535). At Posted the listing gives a posted date and a close date, as the parent R01 listing does [112](#cite:112). Two NIOSH notices posted May 8, 2026 with a close date of June 23, 2026 were shown as Closed [2536](#cite:2536). At Archived stands a NIOSH announcement that expired on November 21, 2025, its listing archived as of December 23, 2025 [556](#cite:556) [557](#cite:557).

Grants.gov's own definitions of the four words were not among the pages read for this guide; each mark rests on a listing that carried the word [2535](#cite:2535) [2536](#cite:2536) [557](#cite:557).

## How this guide uses it

The sections on how [grant](#term:grant) money moves and on the research funders both describe notices, and every route to a competed federal programme ends at one. Programme records give a notice's number, dates and cost-sharing line where a notice exists.


Each programme record also carries a [status label](#term:status-label), which is the guide's own and describes a programme, not one listing. Open: a notice is in force and takes applications, or its next due date is still ahead. Forecast: no open notice, with a forecast or an announced date for the next. Closed: the current notice's last deadline has passed and the programme continues. Expired: the announcement lapsed, was archived or was ended early, and nothing replaces it. [Not-competed](#term:not-competed): the funder says the competition is cancelled, paused or will not be held. [No-current-notice](#term:no-current-notice): none was found for the current cycle, and the funder has not said the programme ended. Formula: money allotted by formula or [block grant](#term:block-grant), with no federal competition a non-profit can enter. Unconfirmed: the pages would not load or did not settle it.


On October 5, 2026 two changes were pending. [OMB](#term:omb)'s [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of May 29, 2026 would require every federal funding opportunity to be posted on Grants.gov, with an exception where public announcement poses a national security risk, and would revise Appendix I [1803](#cite:1803) [1458](#cite:1458). A rule arising from that proposal may not be issued or finalised through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). The [Simpler.Grants.gov](#term:simpler-grants) roadmap gives 2027 as the stage at which that site replaces legacy Grants.gov, with no day or month [1919](#cite:1919).

title: Registrations 101: what has to exist before an application can be sent
one_liner: Before a first federal application the organisation registers in SAM.gov, usually in Grants.gov, and in any system the agency adds, each through a named person.
why_here: The section on the gates and every federal route assume that these registrations already exist. A newcomer trips because the deadline in a notice hides the weeks of registration that come before it, and because the steps fall to different people.

## What it is

A newcomer would assume that an application is a document, finished and then sent. Before anything can be sent the organisation has to exist in several federal systems, and the first is [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov), the registry run by the General Services Administration, where it must hold an active registration to apply as a prime applicant [1897](#cite:1897) [1899](#cite:1899). Registration assigns the [Unique Entity ID (UEI)](#term:uei), which every later registration uses, and a domestic organisation also receives a [CAGE code](#term:cage-code) [1898](#cite:1898) [784](#cite:784). SAM.gov states that there is no charge to get a UEI, to register or to maintain a registration [1898](#cite:1898).

Most agencies then receive applications through [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov), and some add a system of their own, such as [eRA Commons](#term:era-commons) at [NIH](#term:nih) or [Research.gov](#term:research-gov) at [NSF](#term:nsf) [1895](#cite:1895) [1911](#cite:1911) [161](#cite:161). The Department of Justice takes a first form through Grants.gov and the full application in its own [JustGrants](#term:justgrants) [619](#cite:619). NIH describes the SAM.gov entity administrator as the chief financial officer or an authorising official [1909](#cite:1909). The person named in SAM.gov as [Electronic Business Point of Contact](#term:ebiz-poc) registers the organisation on Grants.gov and assigns roles, and someone must hold the [Authorized Organization Representative](#term:authorized-organization-representative) role to submit [1895](#cite:1895). At NIH a Signing Official registers the organisation in eRA Commons [1911](#cite:1911) [1909](#cite:1909). SAM.gov and Grants.gov are entered with a [Login.gov](#term:login-gov) account, which belongs to a person and not to the organisation [1897](#cite:1897) [1965](#cite:1965) [1932](#cite:1932).

The registry gives its own activation time as up to 10 business days, and Grants.gov warns of weeks or months where information is not available or verified [1897](#cite:1897) [1895](#cite:1895). NIH's planning figures are three weeks or more for a first SAM registration, two weeks or more for eRA Commons, one business day or more for Grants.gov, and six weeks or more for the whole set [1909](#cite:1909). NSF advises starting SAM registration at least 90 days before submission [161](#cite:161). The SAM.gov registration lapses unless renewed every 365 days, and under 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) 25.205 an agency may not issue an award, or add funds to one, to an entity out of compliance [1897](#cite:1897) [1899](#cite:1899). A Grants.gov account is deactivated after 365 days of inactivity; NIH states no [renewal](#term:renewal) period for eRA Commons, though the SAM.gov registration it depends on is renewed yearly [1966](#cite:1966) [1909](#cite:1909).

Every [PD/PI](#term:principal-investigator), senior/key person and other significant contributor named on an NIH application needs a personal eRA Commons account, created through the organisation's Signing Official or account administrator, and at NSF each person holds one NSF ID [1910](#cite:1910) [156](#cite:156). For due dates on or after January 25, 2026 NIH requires an [ORCID iD](#term:orcid), a persistent identifier that is free to the researcher, of every person who submits a Common Form, linked to the eRA Commons account [31](#cite:31) [1950](#cite:1950). The [Common Forms](#term:biosketch) are two government-wide disclosure forms, the Biographical Sketch and the [Current and Pending (Other) Support](#term:other-support) form; they are produced in [SciENcv](#term:sciencv), and NIH states that there is no blank template outside it [249](#cite:249) [1943](#cite:1943) [1942](#cite:1942). An organisation that will only be a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) needs less: under 2 CFR 25.300 it must have a UEI and is not required to complete full registration, though with a UEI alone it cannot apply directly for federal awards [1899](#cite:1899) [1900](#cite:1900) [1897](#cite:1897). A person applying on their own behalf through Grants.gov adds an Individual Applicant profile and does not register in SAM.gov [1896](#cite:1896).
picture:
Picture three steps rising to a door marked *submit*. The lowest step is labelled *SAM.gov: UEI and entity registration*, with the entity administrator standing on it [1897](#cite:1897) [1909](#cite:1909). The middle step is *Grants.gov: organisation profile and roles*, with the Electronic Business Point of Contact on it and the Authorized Organization Representative beside the door [1895](#cite:1895). The top step is *the agency's own system*, drawn for NIH as *eRA Commons* with the Signing Official [1911](#cite:1911). Under each step hang two tags, a clock for the stated wait and a loop for renewal. On the first they read *up to 10 business days* and *every 365 days* [1897](#cite:1897). On the second they read *one business day or more*, NIH's estimate, and *account deactivated after 365 days of inactivity* [1909](#cite:1909) [1966](#cite:1966). On the third they read *two weeks or more* and *no renewal period stated* [1909](#cite:1909).

Beside the steps stands a short ladder for the person, its rungs labelled *Login.gov account*, *agency account*, *ORCID iD* and *biosketch in SciENcv* [1910](#cite:1910) [31](#cite:31) [1942](#cite:1942). Low on the first step is a side door marked *UEI only*, where a subrecipient enters; it does not lead to *submit* [1899](#cite:1899) [1897](#cite:1897).

title: Review and decision 101: who reads an application and who decides
one_liner: Reviewers score and advise; an official of the agency decides which applications are paid, at NIH, at NSF and at a programme agency [38](#cite:38) [157](#cite:157) [1112](#cite:1112).
why_here: The research and service routes and the funder records all pass through a review step. A newcomer tends to read a strong score as an award, and the two are separate acts by separate people [38].

body_before:
## What it is

A newcomer tends to assume that a panel of experts reads an application and picks the winners. In federal grant-making the experts advise and an official of the agency decides. [NIH](#term:nih) has two levels of review [38](#cite:38). The first is a [scientific review group](#term:study-section), also called a study section; the [Center for Scientific Review](#term:center-for-scientific-review) organises these groups and clusters them into review branches by discipline [38](#cite:38) [40](#cite:40). The second is the [national advisory council](#term:advisory-council) or board of the institute that would pay, which makes funding recommendations to the [institute or center](#term:institute-or-center) director, and the director decides [38](#cite:38). For most research project applications with due dates from January 25, 2025, a study section works under a simplified framework: Importance of the Research and Rigor and Feasibility are each scored from 1 to 9, and Expertise and Resources is rated sufficient or insufficient [39](#cite:39) [41](#cite:41).

The outcome of review comes back in a [summary statement](#term:summary-statement), which an [AHRQ](#term:ahrq) page last reviewed in October 2014 calls a statement "with the review results" [506](#cite:506). Under practices NIH modified on November 24, 2025 and has continued through the January 2027 council round, 30-35% of applications are discussed in most meetings, the committee's middle third is designated 'competitive but not discussed', and summary statements carry no narrative paragraphs summarising the committee's discussion [126](#cite:126) [16](#cite:16) [84](#cite:84). A [payline](#term:payline) was a cut-off in overall [impact scores](#term:impact-score) that settled which applications an institute would fund, and about half of NIH's institutes, centers and offices had used one [123](#cite:123) [13](#cite:13). Effective with the January 2026 council round they "will not rely on funding paylines in developing pay plans" [13](#cite:13). Each funding policy follows six tenets, among them scientific merit and the availability of funds; [peer review](#term:merit-review) information is weighed "in its entirety", and each institute publishes the factors it uses [123](#cite:123) [15](#cite:15).

At [NSF](#term:nsf), merit review applies two criteria to every proposal, [Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts](#term:intellectual-merit) [157](#cite:157) [160](#cite:160). A [programme officer](#term:program-officer) obtains reviews from ad hoc reviewers, a panel or both, and makes a recommendation to award or decline; the policy guide as printed places final programmatic approval at division or office level [157](#cite:157) [160](#cite:160). After a realignment of December 2025, the pages read do not name the post that now gives it [168](#cite:168) [177](#cite:177). Since December 8, 2025 a full proposal needs at least two reviewers, who may be NSF staff [149](#cite:149). A programme agency such as [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa) has peer reviewers score the project narrative against sections whose points are fixed in the notice [1113](#cite:1113) [1112](#cite:1112). One FY 2026 notice gives 35 points to the implementation approach [1112](#cite:1112). That notice states that "The program office and approving official make the final determination for funding", and that awards over $250,000 need National Advisory Council approval [1112](#cite:1112).

A programme officer is the member of agency staff an applicant may talk to. NIH's programme officials can say whether a plan fits their institute and help interpret review feedback; they do not co-write or edit applications or discuss receipt, referral or review details [92](#cite:92) [120](#cite:120). NSF lists one or more programme officers on each funding opportunity [158](#cite:158). Each agency also reports the share of applications it funds, by its own measure. NIH gave a [success rate](#term:success-rate) of 13.0% for research project [grants](#term:grant) in FY 2025, 8,161 new and [renewal](#term:renewal) awards from 62,592 applications, against 18.5% in FY 2024 [81](#cite:81). NSF's [budget request](#term:budget-request) shows a funding rate of 19% for competitive awards in its FY 2025 plan, 7,400 awards from 38,700 proposals [255](#cite:255).
picture:
Picture three lanes drawn from left to right, labelled NIH, NSF and SAMHSA, each a row of boxes joined by arrows. The NIH lane reads *study section: scores*, then *advisory council: advises*, then *institute or center director: decides* [38](#cite:38). The NSF lane reads *reviewers: ad hoc, panel or both*, then *programme officer: recommendation*, then *division or office: approval, as the guide is printed* [157](#cite:157) [160](#cite:160). The SAMHSA lane reads *peer reviewers: points*, then *programme office and approving official: decide*, with a side box for the National Advisory Council on awards over $250,000 [1112](#cite:1112). Boxes that advise are drawn in outline and boxes that decide are filled, so the filled box is the last in every lane.

Across the top of all three lanes runs one bar, labelled *senior appointee review, [Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332)*. Since that order of August 7, 2025, a senior appointee in each agency reviews new funding opportunity announcements and [discretionary grants](#term:discretionary-grant) before they issue, for consistency with agency priorities and the national interest [246](#cite:246). The bar therefore meets each lane before its first box and again at its last. The order says appointees "shall not ministerially ratify or routinely defer to recommendations of others" [246](#cite:246).

## How this guide uses it

The routes for an NIH research grant, an NSF core proposal and a federal health or behavioural health service grant each carry a review step that rests on this primer, as do the lines on how a funder decides in the funder records. The figure who-decides draws the three lanes, and sections 2 and 4 of the main text give the detail by agency.


Two parts of the NIH lane were unsettled when the guide closed. On August 14, 2026 NIH asked for comment, with responses due October 13, 2026, on a proposal, not in force, to stop reporting final overall impact scores and [percentiles](#term:percentile) and to report three categories instead: 'Most competitive' (top 25%), 'Competitive' (26-50%) and 'Not discussed' (over 50%) [14](#cite:14). On September 22, 2026 the chair of the Senate [Appropriations](#term:appropriations-act) Committee wrote to the [OMB](#term:omb) and NIH Directors about an [executive order](#term:executive-order), reported to be in preparation, that would add a review of NIH grant applications after merit review; the release names no order, and the guide's sweep found none [1892](#cite:1892).

## What it is

A newcomer assumes that eligibility is a question about the project and the people who would carry it out. Many programmes ask an earlier question, about the organisation that applies, and this guide calls the answer standing. [NIH](#term:nih)'s [Institutional Development Award](#term:idea-program) (IDeA) settles it by location, since an institution is eligible only if it is in a state NIH lists [1546](#cite:1546). The Education Department's programme for historically Black colleges and universities ([HBCUs](#term:hbcu)) is open to a class fixed by statute and by a list in regulation, whatever an institution's current enrolment [1649](#cite:1649).

Location is the first kind. [NSF](#term:nsf)'s [EPSCoR](#term:epscor) aims to raise the research competitiveness of targeted jurisdictions, each a state, territory or commonwealth, and Congress authorised IDeA in 1993 for states with historically low NIH [grant](#term:grant) funding [success rates](#term:success-rate) [866](#cite:866) [1545](#cite:1545). Several agencies keep such lists, and the lists are not the same [1517](#cite:1517) [1565](#cite:1565) [1576](#cite:1576) [1543](#cite:1543). NSF names 28 jurisdictions; the Energy Department follows NSF's criteria, and for NASA jurisdiction eligibility is determined by NSF [1517](#cite:1517) [1567](#cite:1567) [1574](#cite:1574). Defense prints 36 entries in the year's notice, USDA lists 19 states for FY 2026, and NIH lists 23 states and Puerto Rico [1565](#cite:1565) [1576](#cite:1576) [1543](#cite:1543). A jurisdiction can be on one list and off another [1517](#cite:1517) [1565](#cite:1565) [1543](#cite:1543) [1576](#cite:1576).

A second kind is a designation, and a third is an institution's profile. HBCUs are listed by state in 34 [CFR](#term:cfr) 608.2, and a [tribal college](#term:tribal-college) or university is defined by statute [1649](#cite:1649) [1617](#cite:1617). A [Hispanic-serving institution (HSI)](#term:hispanic-serving-institution) is an eligible institution whose undergraduate full-time-equivalent enrolment is at least 25 percent Hispanic at the end of the award year before it applies, and the status is shown at application, with no permanent list [1647](#cite:1647) [1642](#cite:1642). Under Titles III and V of the Higher Education Act the Education Department designates each "eligible institution" yearly, from data on needy students and core expenses per student [1596](#cite:1596) [1595](#cite:1595). NASA checks eligibility for its minority university project against its NASA [MSI](#term:minority-serving-institution) List [1629](#cite:1629). The NIH [R15 AREA](#term:r15) award is for an institution whose undergraduate enrolment is greater than its graduate enrolment and which has not received NIH support totalling more than $6 million per year in 4 of the last 7 years [7](#cite:7). NSF counts as predominantly undergraduate an institution that awarded 20 or fewer Ph.D./D.Sci. degrees in NSF-supported fields over the previous two academic years combined, and it opens some programmes only to institutions that the Carnegie Classification does not place in [R1](#term:r1-institution) [254](#cite:254) [832](#cite:832).

For a non-profit the first standing is tax status. [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) lists two non-profit applicant categories, those with [501(c)(3)](#term:section-501c3) status with the IRS and those without, each other than [institutions of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) [2064](#cite:2064). Recognition follows an application to the IRS on [Form 1023](#term:form-1023) or Form 1023-EZ and is decided by [determination letter](#term:determination-letter) [2046](#cite:2046) [2059](#cite:2059). Every section 501(c)(3) organisation is classified as a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) or a [public charity](#term:public-charity), and is presumed a private foundation unless it requests and qualifies for a determination as a public charity [2054](#cite:2054). Three consecutive years without an annual return or notice end the status by [automatic revocation](#term:automatic-revocation) [2057](#cite:2057).

title: The Uniform Guidance 101: the rules beneath every federal award
one_liner: One rulebook, 2 CFR part 200, sets the administrative, cost and audit rules for a federal award, whichever agency makes it [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805).

## What it is

A newcomer tends to read a federal award as an arrangement with one agency, and to expect the rules for spending the money to be that agency's own. Most of them are shared. The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) is the government-wide set of administrative requirements, [cost principles](#term:cost-principles) and audit requirements for federal awards, issued by the [Office of Management and Budget (OMB)](#term:omb) as 2 CFR part 200 [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). It binds the agencies that make awards and, through the terms of each award, recipients and [subrecipients](#term:subrecipient) [1805](#cite:1805).

The part follows an award from start to finish. Before any money moves it fixes what a [notice of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) must contain and in what order [1800](#cite:1800) [1848](#cite:1848). It has the agency review the risk an applicant poses, a review that can end in an award with extra conditions attached [1809](#cite:1809) [1886](#cite:1886). It then lists what the award document must carry, the [termination](#term:termination) provisions among them [1810](#cite:1810).

Once the award is made, the cost principles decide what it may pay for: a cost has to be allowable, and to be allowable it has to be reasonable and allocable, among other tests [1831](#cite:1831). Some changes, such as a change in scope or in key personnel, need [prior approval](#term:prior-approval), which is the agency's written approval before the recipient acts [1815](#cite:1815). A recipient that hands part of the work to another organisation by [subaward](#term:subaward) takes on a list of duties toward it, and the award terms flow down [1823](#cite:1823) [1805](#cite:1805). Financial reports are collected no less than annually and no more often than quarterly [1820](#cite:1820). A non-federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more in federal awards during its fiscal year must have a [single audit](#term:single-audit), which is filed with the [Federal Audit Clearinghouse](#term:federal-audit-clearinghouse) [1845](#cite:1845) [1846](#cite:1846).

The part also governs the end of an award. Section 200.340 lists four ways an award may be terminated: the recipient's failure to comply, the recipient's consent, the recipient's own written notice, and the terms of the award itself [1801](#cite:1801). At [closeout](#term:closeout) a recipient submits all reports and liquidates its financial obligations no later than 120 calendar days after the end of the [period of performance](#term:budget-period) [1830](#cite:1830). Where a federal statute or regulation conflicts with the part, the statute or regulation governs [1805](#cite:1805).

title: Who applies 101: the organisation, the investigator, the fellow
one_liner: On most federal awards an organisation applies and signs, the investigator is named in it, and only some fellowships are applied for by the person.
why_here: The sections on how grant money moves and on money that follows a person, and every route for a fellowship, a career award or a training grant, assume the reader knows who the applicant is. A newcomer trips because the name of an award does not say who submits it.

## What it is

A newcomer tends to assume that the researcher with the idea is the applicant. On most federal awards an organisation applies and the investigator is named in its application; [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) says that most [grants](#term:grant) are for organisations and that individuals can apply for opportunities from certain federal agencies [1896](#cite:1896) [1895](#cite:1895). [NSF](#term:nsf) invites proposals from all qualified scientists, engineers and educators through an eligible organisation, and unaffiliated individuals are not eligible for direct funding [158](#cite:158) [156](#cite:156). At [NIH](#term:nih) any individual with the skills, knowledge and resources to carry out the research may be the programme director/[principal investigator](#term:principal-investigator), shortened to PD/PI, while the organisation holds the registrations [4](#cite:4) [117](#cite:117).

The organisation also signs: on Grants.gov someone must hold the [Authorized Organization Representative (AOR)](#term:authorized-organization-representative) role to submit, and the roles are assigned by the contact named in the organisation's [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) registration [1895](#cite:1895). At NIH a Signing Official, a business official with authority to bind the organisation, registers it in [eRA Commons](#term:era-commons) and creates the accounts of its PD/PIs [1911](#cite:1911) [1909](#cite:1909) [1910](#cite:1910). NSF's Authorized Organizational Representative signs a proposal sent through Grants.gov and makes nine certifications under NSF's policy guide [161](#cite:161) [257](#cite:257). NIH's help and planning pages send an applicant first to the organisation's own [office of sponsored research](#term:sponsored-programs-office), here called the sponsored programmes office, which explains the process and roles and sets up system accounts [146](#cite:146) [119](#cite:119).

Money meant for one person's training does not settle who applies, because each programme fixes who submits [818](#cite:818) [784](#cite:784) [1016](#cite:1016) [825](#cite:825). In NSF's Graduate Research Fellowship the student applies directly, though the funds are awarded to the institution where the fellow enrols [818](#cite:818). NSF's biology postdoctoral fellowship is submitted by the individual and awarded directly to the fellow [837](#cite:837). For an NIH [F31](#term:f-award) or F32 fellowship the organisation applies with the person named, and an institution likewise submits a mentored career development (K) application for a named candidate [784](#cite:784) [737](#cite:737) [744](#cite:744). In the [T32](#term:t32) training grant the person leaves the application altogether: an institution applies through a programme director and appoints trainees, who receive NIH [stipends](#term:stipend) and do not apply to the funder [750](#cite:750) [732](#cite:732). NIH sets the stipends for these National Research Service Awards ([NRSA](#term:nrsa)) once a fiscal year, and for awards made with FY 2026 funds the predoctoral level is $29,364 [732](#cite:732).

Some foundation awards put a [nomination](#term:institutional-nomination) before any application. The Packard Foundation invited 50 institutions to nominate for its 2026 fellowships, up to two each through the president, and a faculty member elsewhere has no route in [2149](#cite:2149). Because the Dreyfus Foundation takes one nomination per institution a year and Pew one nominee from each participating institution, the institution runs an internal selection and the nominee then completes the funder's own application [2146](#cite:2146) [2174](#cite:2174) [2149](#cite:2149). An organisation can also take part in a federal award without applying for it: a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) receives a [subaward](#term:subaward) from a [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity), the body that passes federal money on, to carry out part of the award, and the federal terms flow down to it [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). Where agencies stand on a [fiscally sponsored](#term:fiscal-sponsorship) applicant was read on two pages only, and neither accepts one [2065](#cite:2065) [648](#cite:648). The Arts Endowment bars an organisation without its own non-profit status from applying through a fiscal sponsor, and an [NEH](#term:neh) notice of March 12, 2026 makes fiscal sponsors applying on behalf of an ineligible organisation ineligible; other agencies' rules were not checked [2065](#cite:2065) [648](#cite:648) [2047](#cite:2047).
